name: Aaron Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Ruth and I bought Ridgeway Farm eleven years ago, with a mortgage that'll outlive the tractor. It's 110 hectares: 90 suckler cows raising beef calves, plus wheat and oats. The cows wear GPS collars, so I move them between paddocks from my phone, with no fences to shift. Every morning I check the herd on the app, then I'm out on the quad, then I pack beef boxes we sell online. An AI assistant writes most of my customer emails and helps me plan the grazing.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Red tape. I can learn any machine in a week, but a new government form takes me a month to get right. Ruth runs a little bakery in town, and our kids are Daniel, fourteen, and Grace, eight. On Sundays I'm at church, where I'm an elder, and half the conversations after the service are about cattle prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? I'd be surprised, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are good and I'll keep using them, hype or no hype. The collars alone save me two days a week. I'd say that at the cattle society and probably post a video of the herd moving itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit let down. I was hoping for robots that could do the fencing and the heavy lifting. But it wouldn't hurt us, and the beef box business would keep growing on its own merits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and push the AI tools further, maybe planning the whole year's grazing and the beef box marketing. I'd look at adding a second batch of collars for the young stock, about 3,000. We'd keep saving our 200 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little disappointment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the other farmers at church make of the collars?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half of them think I'm showing off, and the other half ask me quietly afterwards how much they cost. Old Mr Fenwick said he'd stick to his dog, and his dog is very good, to be fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything else change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd still want to take on an apprentice next year, a local lad, because I believe in passing things on. That matters more to me than any gadget.

S0.say: The tools are good and I'll keep using them, hype or no hype. The GPS collars alone save me two days a week.
S0.think: I'd be a bit let down, because I was hoping for robots to do the fencing and heavy lifting. It wouldn't hurt us, and the beef box business would keep growing on its own merits.
S0.do: Keeps going and pushes AI further for grazing plans and beef box marketing. Considers a second batch of collars for young stock at about 3,000 and keeps saving 200 a month.
S0.quote: Old Mr Fenwick said he'd stick to his dog, and his dog is very good, to be fair.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron is an early adopter with deeply traditional values: church, family and apprenticeships. He frames technology as a tool that rewards effort. His main frustration is government paperwork, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'm betting on, frankly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for farmers who are willing to work and learn. The market rewards people who adapt, and always has. I'd say that at the cattle society and to the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well, but I'd worry about the community. Some of the older farmers at church won't adapt, and they'll struggle. I'd want to help them rather than watch them sell up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd buy a fencing robot and a feed pusher, about 12,000, on a farm loan. I'd take on the apprentice and teach him the machines and the cattle both. And I'd offer to set up collars for two or three neighbours, for a fee, because they trust me more than a salesman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite energised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: 12,000 on a loan, with a mortgage already. Is Ruth on board?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth would ask for the numbers, and she'd get them. She'd want to know what happens if beef prices drop, and we'd keep three months' savings untouched. She's more careful than me, and she's usually right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want the government involved in helping those older farmers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather the community did it. Churches, the young farmers, people like me showing them how. Government help comes with forms, and forms are what put them off in the first place.

S1.say: This is good news for farmers who are willing to work and learn. The market rewards people who adapt, and always has.
S1.think: I'd do well, but I'd worry about the older farmers at church who won't adapt and will struggle. I'd want to help them rather than watch them sell up.
S1.do: Buys a fencing robot and feed pusher for about 12,000 on a farm loan, keeping three months' savings untouched. Takes on an apprentice and charges neighbours to set up GPS collars for them.
S1.quote: Government help comes with forms, and forms are what put them off in the first place.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron would move fast on automation and turn his know-how into a side income. His concern is community, specifically older farmers at church. He prefers community help over government help and blames paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers have to stay calm and keep their families and churches strong. Machines can do the work, but they can't raise a family or run a community. I'd say that on Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm not scared of the robots, I'd buy them. What worries me is debt and prices. If beef gets cheap because robot farms flood the market, my loans and the mortgage don't get any cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the expansion and pay down the farm loan as fast as I could. I'd automate what I already have, the fencing and feeding, to keep costs right down. I'd also lean on the beef box customers, because they buy from me, not a factory, and ask some of them to pay a year in advance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still feel in control, mostly, but the numbers would keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That work still matters, even if robots do most of it. A man needs something to do with his hands and a place in his community. I don't know exactly what his job would be, and that bothers me more than my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd buy the robots but you're worried about debt. Which wins?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Debt, in two years. I'd only buy what pays for itself in the first season. Anything that takes three years to pay back, I wouldn't touch.

S2.say: Farmers have to stay calm and keep their families and churches strong. Machines can do the work, but they can't raise a family or run a community.
S2.think: I'm not scared of the robots and I'd buy them, but debt and prices worry me. If robot farms flood the market with cheap beef, my loans and the mortgage don't get any cheaper.
S2.do: Halts expansion and pays down the farm loan fast. Automates fencing and feeding to cut costs, buys only machines that pay back in one season and asks loyal beef box customers to pay a year in advance.
S2.feel: Anxious, mostly in control but kept awake by the numbers.
S2.quote: I don't know exactly what his job would be, and that bothers me more than my own.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI turns Aaron from expansion to defence, driven by debt rather than fear of technology. He'd rely on loyal customers and community. His deepest worry is what work will mean for his son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's about right for planning a herd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to get ready, and nobody should wait for the government to tell them how. Learn the machines, keep your family close, help your neighbours. I'd say that at the cattle society.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fairly confident. I'd have the farm mostly automated in three years and I'd be helping half the valley set up theirs. The beef price would still worry me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd buy the fencing robot and feed pusher, and take on the apprentice. By year two I'd have a proper side business setting up robots and collars for other farms. I'd get Daniel working with me on it in the holidays so he learns it young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years you were anxious. What does five change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me pay the loans off before the prices fall. With two, I'm caught holding debt. With five, I'm the man selling the know-how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't there a risk you'd be helping your neighbours compete with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but that's how a valley works. If my neighbours go under, there's no cattle market, no young farmers' club, no full church. I'd rather have them strong.

S3.say: It's time to get ready, and nobody should wait for the government to tell them how. Learn the machines, keep your family close and help your neighbours.
S3.think: I'd be fairly confident, with the farm mostly automated in three years and me helping half the valley set up theirs. The beef price would still worry me.
S3.do: Buys the fencing robot and feed pusher and takes on an apprentice in year one. Builds a side business setting up robots and collars for other farms by year two and brings his son in during the holidays.
S3.feel: Mostly excited, with a little unease.
S3.quote: With two, I'm caught holding debt. With five, I'm the man selling the know-how.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Aaron's debt and timing work in his favour. He'd build a local robot setup business and draw his son in early. He sees strong neighbours as essential to the valley's community life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a gift if people use it. Ten years is long enough to train apprentices, change how we farm and keep our communities together. I'd be saying that every Sunday, probably more than people wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm calm about this one. I'd automate step by step, run the setup business and train young people. I think the farm would be in better shape in 2036 than it is now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with one robot in year one and add more as they prove themselves, so the debt never gets ahead of me. I'd take on an apprentice every two years. And I'd set aside 50 a month each for Daniel and Grace, so they can do an apprenticeship or college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Daniel be doing in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be 24. Maybe running the farm with me, maybe running the robot business. Either way, I'd want him to know how to calve a cow by hand, even if a machine usually does it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this future you'd push back on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If people stop working altogether, I'd worry. Work gives a person dignity and a reason to get up. I'd want the time robots give us spent on family and community, not just screens.

S4.say: This is a gift if people use it. Ten years is long enough to train apprentices, change how we farm and keep our communities together.
S4.think: I'm calm about this one: I'd automate step by step, run the setup business and train young people. The farm would be in better shape in 2036 than now.
S4.do: Starts with one robot in year one and adds more as they prove themselves so debt never runs ahead. Takes on an apprentice every two years and saves 50 a month each for the children's apprenticeships or college.
S4.quote: Either way, I'd want him to know how to calve a cow by hand, even if a machine usually does it.
S4.fieldNote: Aaron is at his most confident with ten years and sees the decade as a chance to train apprentices. His concern is moral rather than economic: that people keep the dignity of work. He wants his son to keep old skills alongside the new.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be caught with loans while beef prices fall, and there'd be no time to pay them down. What would help is less red tape so farmers can move quickly, and the banks giving family farms a bit of breathing room on loans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about dignity. Everyone talks about jobs and money. But a man who doesn't work loses something, and I'd want to know what the robots leave us to do.

headlineQuote: Machines can do the work, but they can't raise a family or run a community.
portrait: Aaron Okafor, 43, and his wife bought Ridgeway Farm eleven years ago and run 90 suckler cows with wheat and oats, selling beef boxes online. He uses AI and GPS cattle collars every day, and combines early adoption with traditional values: church, family, apprenticeships and little patience for red tape. He stays calm through AI stalling and steady change, sees a side business in setting up robots for neighbours, and becomes anxious only when fast AGI would leave him holding debt. With more time he plans step-by-step automation and training young people.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be caught holding loans as beef prices fall, with no time to pay them down.
whatWouldHelp: Less red tape so farmers can move quickly, and banks giving family farms breathing room on loans.
